references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] You must notify your council or the NSW Food Authority if you intend to operate a food business. Retail food outlets such as cafes, restaurants, takeaways, food trucks and retail bakeries, school canteens, children's services and manufacturers or caterers that sell directly to consumers notify their council. Manufacturers, wholesalers, catering not sold by retail, food importers not selling by retail and similar businesses notify the NSW Food Authority. The online Food Business Notification form is at formsfa.bfs.dpi.nsw.gov.au/forms/12120. The Food Authority's inspection or audit fee for 2026-27 is $370 an hour. Legislation: Food Act 2003 (NSW) and Food Regulation 2025 (NSW).
references.interpretation: Every NSW food business must notify before it trades; most retail businesses notify their council, which also inspects and charges fees. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.section: Who needs a Food Safety Supervisor
references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Retail, hospitality and food service businesses must appoint at least one Food Safety Supervisor per premises when the food they prepare and serve is ready to eat, potentially hazardous (needs temperature control) and not sold in the supplier's original package. Examples include cafes, restaurants, takeaways, pubs and clubs with food, mobile vendors, caterers, supermarkets, delis and school canteens. Food Safety Supervisor certificates expire 5 years from issue; when one expires the business has 30 days to renew the training or appoint another certified supervisor.
references.interpretation: Businesses that prepare and serve unpackaged ready-to-eat food need a certified Food Safety Supervisor at each premises. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] NSW liquor licence types include small bar (up to 120 patrons, no gaming or takeaway), general bar, on-premises (alcohol sold where another product or service is the main business, such as a restaurant), club, hotel, producer or wholesaler, packaged liquor (bottle shops), and limited licences for special events, trade fairs and functions. Some situations, such as BYO restaurants, may not need a licence.
references.interpretation: Selling or supplying alcohol in NSW needs a licence from Liquor & Gaming NSW unless an exemption applies. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Check whether you need a licence, choose a licence type, check whether you need council development approval first, prepare documents such as a recent National Police Check, ASIC company extracts and RSA and licensee training, and a Statement of Risks and Potential Effects where required, then lodge online through the NSW OneGov liquor portal. After lodging you generally notify stakeholders such as NSW Police, the local consent authority and occupiers of nearby buildings. The application is advertised for up to 30 days (14 days for straightforward restaurants). A complete application is generally decided within 7 working days, or up to 12 weeks if more information is needed or there are objections.
references.interpretation: The NSW liquor licence process: choose a type, lodge online, notify stakeholders, public consultation, decision. Captured on 2026-10-12 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

rule_sets.title: New South Wales: business licences, insurance and tax
rule_sets.description: Licences, notifications, insurance and tax most NSW businesses check: food, liquor, footpath dining, tobacco, signs, live music, workers' insurance and payroll tax.
limitations: Built from NSW Government, NSW Health, Liquor & Gaming NSW, icare, Revenue NSW and business.gov.au web pages, not from the Acts themselves.
